title: Check out these 6 seriously haunted bars and restaurants in Louisville
excerpt: Louisville is home to several restaurants and bars that are believed to be haunted. Grab a bite to eat at one of these haunted places.
content:
Oct. 19, 2026, 5:02 a.m. ET

  • Several establishments in Louisville, Kentucky, are known for reported paranormal activity and ghost sightings.
  • The Brown Hotel and The Seelbach Hilton Hotel are two historic downtown hotels with long-standing ghost stories.
  • Restaurants and bars along Whiskey Row, such as Doc Crow's and Troll Pub, are considered hotbeds for paranormal events.
  • Even a local brewery, 3rd Turn Brewing, and a pizzeria, Pizza Lupo, have reported unexplainable occurrences.

Louisville is home to some spooky sites.

Several Derby City establishments often come up on lists of haunted places, such as Haunted Room Co.'s website that reads, "Louisville has more than its fair share of creepy tales to tell."

Haunted Room, a resource for ghost hunts around the country, calls out The Brennan House, The Belle of Louisville, Cave Hill Cemetery, and the Louisville Palace Theatre as just a few of the most ghostly venues in town.

These eerie places aren't confined to Louisville. Two of Kentucky's most famous distilleries also show some spooky spirit, as both Buffalo Trace in Frankfort and Wild Turkey in Lawrenceburg were previously named among the most haunted distilleries in the U.S, according to a 2025 list from Wine Enthusiast.

Buffalo Trace's popular Blanton's line of bourbon is named for Albert Blanton, a company president in the early 1920s who spent his life around the property, and passed away at the distillery, Matt Higgins, visitor services general manager with Buffalo Trace, told Wine Enthusiast.

"Some believe the spirit of Blanton still remains at the distillery," the Wine Enthusiast story states. "Multiple guests have reported seeing an older man matching the description of Blanton in and around the warehouses, bottling hall, and Stony Point, Blanton’s former residence."

As for Wild Turkey, the iconic distillery was featured on "Ghost Hunters," a Syfy channel TV show in 2015, when ghost hunters investigated the grounds of Wild Turkey after employees reported hearing weird sounds, such as typewriters, footsteps, doors opening and closing, and voices at the distillery.

As Halloween nears, you'll find several options for pop-ups bars, complete with Halloween decorations and themed cocktails, around Louisville. But, if you're looking to grab a drink or bite at a truly spooky place, Louisville has options for that, too.

Mysteriously, several famously haunted bars, including The Silver Dollar, Hilltop Tavern, Meta, and Phoenix Hill Tavern, have all closed in recent years. However, there could be new "life" for at least one ghost. Voilà Cocktail Bar opened Oct. 15 at the former site of Meta, so we'll have to check back in to see if Meta's resident ghost (a former dancer named Paula) shows up at the new digs.

Read on for details about five haunted places to check out in Louisville's food scene.

Five haunted bars, restaurants in Louisville, Ky.

3rd Turn Brewing

Details: 10408 Watterson Trail, Jeffersontown, Ky., 3rdturnbrewing.com

This brewery located inside a former church built in 1878 at 10408 Watterson Trail in Jeffersontown has "its fair share of haunted tales," according to an October 2025 Facebook post.

The tales include "mysterious notes and voices calling your name" and "a corner that changes temperature on its own, and even a glass that shattered out of nowhere (that wasn’t even ours)."

As for the note in question, the owners of 3rd Turn Brewing found a note left on a table from the previous owners that read, "Hey, little girl, please be nice to the new owners." 

That note is now framed and hangs up at the brewery. 

Before 3rd Turn opened in 2015, the site operated as a Moose Lodge for 60 years.

3rd Turn Brewing co-owner Greg Hayden previously told The Courier Journal he's never been one to believe in the supernatural, and ghosts were "just your brain trying to make sense of random things it sees, like how you see pictures in the clouds."

"But, I will say, some of the stuff we've seen, it gets harder and harder to explain," he said.

The Brown Hotel

Details: 335 W. Broadway, Louisville, Ky., brownhotel.com

The Brown Hotel in downtown Louisville sits in a building with history dating back to 1923, leaving plenty of years for ghost stories to float around, many of which clue in on the hotel’s namesake and builder, J. Graham Brown.

The hotel paused operations after Brown’s death in 1969 and reopened more than a decade later, but Brown may still like to check up on things, according to decades of reports.

"It is very common for Mr. Brown’s spirit, to make an appearance during busy times at the hotel including Derby week and during receptions or conventions being held at the hotel," states Haunted Room Co.'s website. "A number of staff say that they have locked eyes with the ghost at which point he may or may not nod his approval before vanishing."

His apparition usually appears standing in what was Brown's favorite spot, under the arch on the mezzanine, and with the faint smell of cigars.

You don't have to stay at The Brown Hotel to get a taste of the spookiness. The hotel is home to dining areas such as the Lobby Bar & Grill and J. Graham’s Café, where you can dig into the legendary Hot Brown while keeping a look out for ghosts.

Doc Crow's Smokehouse and Raw Bar

Details: 127 W. Main St., Louisville, Ky., doccrows.com

Located next to Old Forester Distilling Co., this restaurant is one of several Whiskey Row spots that's a "hotbed for paranormal activity," according to the Kentucky Distillers' Association website.

At the building where Doc Crow's sits, 127 W. Main St., it's believed Union General William “Bull” Nelson was shot and killed by Army General Jefferson C. Davis in 1862. The "deadly confrontation" may still linger today, as Doc Crow's has been home to "reports of a table barging through a locked door unassisted, flying glassware and menus placing themselves on tables have been made," reads the Kentucky Distillers' Association website.

The Whiskey Row thrills continue at Patrick O’Sheas Irish Pub, 123 W. Main St., which is next door to Doc Crow's, where a ghost named Willy, who is believed to have been killed by a load of bourbon barrels, has been said to haunt the area.

Old Seelbach Bar at The Seelbach Hilton Hotel

Details: 500 S. 4th St., Louisville, Ky., seelbachhilton.com

At The Seelbach Hilton Hotel, 500 S. 4th St. in downtown Louisville. the feeling of goosebumps isn't uncommon.

The historic hotel in downtown Louisville is said to experience regular visits from The Lady in Blue, the nickname for a widow "who either jumped or fell to her death down a service elevator shaft," as a U.S. News & World Report story about "The 27 most haunted hotels in America" stated.

"Rumors have circulated about her lingering presence here since reported sightings of a mysterious blue-clad figure in 1987," the U.S. News & World Report story continued. "Some hotel guests today say they've felt cold spots or caught the unexplained aroma of perfume during their stay."

Haunted areas abound at the hotel, famous for visits from gangster Al Capone and "The Great Gatsby" author F. Scott Fitzgerald, and you can catch a glimpse at the Old Seelbach Bar, an early 1900s bar that's a stop on the Urban Bourbon Trail. The most popular drink here is the Old Fashioned, which is priced at $15 and made with Elijah Craig bourbon.

"The building is very haunted," night security guard Patrick Rhodes previously told the Courier Journal. "Between Al Capone and the gangsters (staying here), World War I and II and the Great Depression and the age of the building, there's lots of different things that have happened here."

Pizza Lupo

Details: 1540 Frankfort Ave., Louisville, Ky., pizzalupo.com

One of Louisville's favorite pizzerias serves the popular "Sting Like a Bee" pie, and might bring bits of spooky sensations.

There's an old haunted well in the basement of Pizza Lupo, 1540 Frankfort Ave., where solid items have been known to fly off shelves and mimics of servers' voices, sneezes and hiccups can sometimes be heard. The well leads to the original Louisville cistern and a child's doll sits at the bottom, The Courier Journal previously reported.

Pizza Lupo moved into the 150-year-old building in 2017 and owner Max Balliet previously told The Courier Journal that he's lost count of how many unexplainable occurrences have happened there.

Troll Pub Under the Bridge

Details: 150 W. Washington St., Louisville, Ky., trollpub.com/louisville

The Troll Pub's mascot, named Louie, may look a little funny, but he's not the spooky part of this Whiskey Row subterranean sports bar.

The site at 150 W. Washington St. has a history of tragic events, as it was the original Galt House hotel in 1834. A fire ravaged the building in 1865 and destroyed the hotel and the Ohio River flood of 1937 put Washington Street, and the underground space, under water, as Troll Pub's website states.

When the bar and restaurant opened in 2011, it did so after "months of digging out mounds and mounds of dirt."

In the basement area shared between Doc Crow’s and Troll Pub, employees of both restaurants "have spotted a nun, believed to have perished during the Galt House fire in 1865," according to a Flaviar story about haunted places around Whiskey Row.

Today, the eatery leans into its troll theme more than any spooky nods with menu items such as Louie The Troll's Signature Beer Cheese, Troll's Drunken Cheesecake and the Troll Fashion, the pub's take on an Old Fashioned.
